title: Remembering Death
description: Fifteen minutes with the oldest of reflections. Not to be afraid, but to live with more presence.

segments.say: Find a comfortable position and close your eyes.
Breathe slowly a few times. Let the body settle.
This is an old practice. The Buddha asked monks to remember death with every breath.
Not to be afraid. But because when we remember time is short, what matters becomes clear.
If today is a day of grief or of great fragility, it is fine to leave this practice for another time.
Feel the breath. It comes in, and goes out.
One day, there will be a last out-breath. It is the one certainty we all share.
Feel this breath, knowing it is one of the ones you have.
Now, slowly, repeat each reflection silently after me.
My body will grow old. There is no avoiding it.
My body will fall ill. There is no avoiding it.
I will die. There is no avoiding it.
Everyone and everything I love will change, and I will be parted from them.
My actions are my only inheritance. What I do is what remains.
Notice what comes up. Maybe resistance, sadness, or a strange calm. All of it is welcome.
Now ask yourself, without hurry: if my time is limited, what really matters?
Let the answer come from the body, not the head.
Bring to mind someone you love. Remember that your time together is limited too.
Feel the tenderness in that.
Now come back to the breath. It is still here. You are still here.
What a strange and precious thing, to be alive right now.
Carry this into the rest of your day. Not as a weight, but as gratitude.
When you are ready, open your eyes.
